categories.description:
A lift table raises and lowers a load so that people can work on it, or move it, at a comfortable height instead of bending, reaching or lifting by hand. They are used at assembly stations, packing lines, machine tools, loading areas and anywhere heavy parts are handled repeatedly.

Most lift tables use a scissor mechanism driven by a hydraulic cylinder, but the category also includes single-column mobile tables, pneumatic air-bag lifts, multi-stage tables for extra height, and tables that tilt or rotate the load as well as lifting it. Power ranges from a simple foot pump to electric, air and battery units.

Browse by type or by power source below, compare models from each manufacturer, and request quotes from distributors who sell and service them.

Scissor lift tables raise a platform on one or more pairs of crossed steel legs. As a hydraulic cylinder or air bag pushes the legs toward vertical, the platform rises while staying level. The design folds down to a compact lowered height and spreads the load across a wide base, which is why it is the most common lift table construction.

Stationary scissor tables are bolted or set in place at a workstation and are typically electric-hydraulic for frequent cycling. Key specifications to compare are capacity, platform size, lowered height, vertical travel and the rated duty cycle. For loads that must be rolled on with a pallet jack, look at low-profile or floor-level scissor tables.

how_to_choose.title: Start with how the load arrives
how_to_choose.text: A standard scissor table sits 7 to 12 inches off the floor, so anything rolled on with a pallet jack will not reach it. If loads arrive on a jack or a cart, you need a low-profile or floor-level table — those go down to about a quarter of an inch — or a pit-mounted install.

how_to_choose.title: Check capacity at full height, not just the badge
how_to_choose.text: A rating is usually quoted at the lowered position. Some designs derate as the legs approach vertical, and off-centre or edge loading derates them further. If the load will sit toward one end of the platform, ask for the rating in that condition.

how_to_choose.title: Match the duty cycle to how often it runs
how_to_choose.text: A table cycling every two minutes on an assembly line needs a different pump and motor from one raised twice a shift. Duty cycle is the specification most often overlooked and the one that decides whether the table is still working in five years.

how_to_choose.title: Single, double or triple scissor
how_to_choose.text: A single scissor’s travel is limited by its lowered height. Stacking mechanisms buys height — this category reaches past fifty feet — at the cost of footprint, stability at full extension and price. Do not buy travel you will not use.

categories.description:
Mobile lift tables combine a lifting platform with casters so a load can be raised to working height and then moved to where it is needed. They are often called lift carts or portable lift tables, and are used to carry dies, parts, tooling and cartons between workstations, shelves and machines.

Most are manually operated with a foot pump, which keeps them self-contained and simple, while heavier or higher-cycle models use battery power. When comparing mobile tables, look at capacity, deck size, lowered and raised height, caster size and type, and whether the casters lock. Check that the lowered height suits the shelf, bench or machine the table will load from.

how_to_choose.title: Pick the power source from the cycle rate
how_to_choose.text: Manual hydraulic tables are raised by a foot pump — entirely self-contained, nothing to charge, and tiring if the table is raised many times a day. Battery tables suit repeated cycling and heavier loads. This category runs from 200 to 6,000 lb, and the heavier end is almost always powered.

how_to_choose.title: Decide whether it moves loaded or empty
how_to_choose.text: Pushing a loaded table takes considerably more force than pushing an empty one, and it changes the caster size, the wheel material and the floor surface you can use. If it will be moved loaded, say so when specifying.

how_to_choose.title: Insist on a floor lock
how_to_choose.text: A table that rolls while somebody is loading it is a hazard, not an inconvenience. Foot-operated floor locks or brake casters are standard on good mobile tables and should not be treated as an option.

how_to_choose.title: Measure the doorways
how_to_choose.text: Overall width, not platform width, is what has to pass through an aisle, a doorway and into a lift. Mobile tables are bought to travel, and the narrowest point on their route is the real constraint.

categories.description:
Post lift tables raise the deck on a single central hydraulic column rather than a scissor mechanism. With nothing folding beneath the deck, the column sits in the middle of a compact base, and the deck can often rotate freely around it and lock at any height, which suits welding, machining and assembly work where the operator turns the part while working on it.

Most post lift tables are mobile, rolling on casters with a floor lock, and they typically offer a working-height range rather than floor-level loading, because the column and base set a minimum lowered height. Compare deck size and shape, capacity, lowered and raised height, how the deck rotates and locks, and whether the table is powered by a foot pump, electric motor, air or battery.

categories.path: Lift Tables > Double Scissor Lift Tables
categories.description:
Double scissor lift tables stack two scissor mechanisms on top of each other to reach a much greater raised height from the same compact footprint. Where a single scissor table may lift a load to around waist or chest height, a double scissor design can reach mezzanines, raised work platforms and tall machine loading points.

Designs with three or more scissor stages exist for even greater travel. Because the extra height changes how the table carries a load, compare capacity at full height, platform stability, the length of the platform relative to its travel, and the safety features required for the height involved, such as toe guards, skirts and handrails.

Rotating lift tables add a turntable top to a lifting base, so the operator can bring any side of the load to the front instead of walking around it or reaching across it. They are common at welding, assembly and packing stations and wherever a large part needs work on several faces.

Rotation may be free-spinning with a lock, indexed at set positions, or powered. Some mobile tables also rotate their deck a full 360 degrees and lock it at any height. When comparing models, check how the top locks in position, whether it rotates at every height, and how capacity is rated when the load sits off-center on the turntable.

Tilt tables angle the platform toward the operator so that the contents of a bin, box or gaylord can be reached without leaning over the side. Lift-and-tilt tables combine vertical lifting with tilting, letting the load be raised to working height and then presented at an angle.

They are widely used for parts picking, container unloading and kitting, where repeatedly reaching into the bottom of a deep container is a common cause of strain. Compare the tilt angle, whether the table lifts as well as tilts, how the load is retained when angled, and the capacity rating at full tilt.

how_to_choose.title: Work out the angle from the container, not the catalogue
how_to_choose.text: Tilt angle is set by how deep the container is and how far the operator would otherwise have to reach. Shallow totes may need 30 degrees; deep stillages and gaylords often need 45 or more. Too little tilt and the table solves nothing.

how_to_choose.title: Decide whether you also need height
how_to_choose.text: A tilt-only table angles the load at a fixed height. A lift-and-tilt does both, which is what most picking and kitting stations actually need — the operator wants the work at the right height and angled toward them at the same time.

how_to_choose.title: Make sure the load cannot slide
how_to_choose.text: Angling a load is only safe if something holds it. Look for a lip, backstop or retaining edge rated for the load, and confirm it works with your container rather than only with a pallet.

how_to_choose.title: Read the capacity at full tilt
how_to_choose.text: Ratings are sometimes quoted flat. The load a tilter can hold at maximum angle is the number that matters, because that is the position it will spend its working life in.

categories.description:
Pallet lift tables raise a full pallet to a comfortable loading or unloading height. They include pallet positioners built as lifting tables: platforms that rise automatically as the load gets lighter, or that the operator raises in steps, so the top layer always stays at the same working height.

Spring and pneumatic pallet positioners respond to the weight on them without controls, while hydraulic and air-powered models are raised on demand. Many include a turntable so the operator can rotate the pallet rather than reach across it. Compare capacity, platform size relative to the pallets used, lowered height, and how the pallet is loaded, whether by forklift or pallet jack.

categories.path: Lift Tables > Low Profile Lift Tables
categories.description:
Low profile lift tables are built to fold down to a very low lowered height, low enough that a pallet jack can roll a load straight onto the platform, often with a short ramp. That removes the need for a forklift to place the load and avoids cutting a pit into the floor.

They are used at packing, shipping and assembly stations where loads arrive on pallet jacks. Because the mechanism has to fit in very little space, compare the actual lowered height, ramp length and slope, capacity, vertical travel, and whether the platform shape leaves room for the pallet jack forks.

categories.path: Lift Tables > Floor Level Lift Tables
categories.description:
Floor level lift tables, sometimes called ground entry or floor height lifts, lower their platform all the way to the floor so a pallet jack or hand cart can roll straight on with no ramp and no pit. Many use a U-shaped or E-shaped platform with an open side so the pallet jack can be driven in and withdrawn once the pallet is down.

They suit sites where loads arrive by pallet jack and a pit is not practical. Compare the platform opening width against the pallets and jacks in use, the capacity, the vertical travel, and how the table keeps a pallet stable when the platform has an open side.

categories.path: Lift Tables > Heavy Duty Lift Tables
categories.description:
Heavy duty lift tables are built for loads beyond the range of typical workstation tables. On this site the category covers tables rated for 6,000 lb or more, used for dies, molds, machinery components, heavy castings and full loads of dense material.

At higher capacities, construction details matter as much as the headline rating. Compare the capacity at full raised height, whether the rating allows for off-center or edge loading, the platform deflection, the number and size of cylinders, and whether the table is rated for rolling loads onto it. Many heavy duty tables are built to order around the application.

categories.path: Lift Tables > Stainless Steel Lift Tables
categories.description:
Stainless steel lift tables are made for environments where painted carbon steel would corrode or contaminate the work area, including food and beverage processing, pharmaceutical manufacturing, cleanrooms and washdown areas. Stainless construction resists rust and stands up to repeated cleaning with water and chemical cleaners.

Tables may be fully stainless or use stainless platforms and exposed parts on a coated base. Compare which components are stainless and in what grade, whether hydraulic and electrical parts are sealed for washdown, whether a food-grade hydraulic fluid is used, and how easy the design is to clean around the scissor legs and base.

Hydraulic lift tables use a cylinder filled with hydraulic fluid to raise the platform, and they are the most widely used type. The fluid can be pressurized by a hand or foot pump, an electric motor, an air motor, or a battery-powered pump, so hydraulic tables cover everything from simple manual carts to high-cycle production lifts.

Hydraulics give smooth, controlled lifting and can hold a load at any height. When comparing hydraulic tables, look at how the pump is powered, how fast the table raises and lowers, whether lowering speed is adjustable, and which safety features are fitted, such as velocity fuses that limit descent if a hose fails.

how_to_choose.title: Decide how the pump is powered
how_to_choose.text: Electric-hydraulic suits frequent cycling and is the default on a production line. A hand or foot pump is self-contained and fine for occasional use. Air-over-hydraulic needs no electricity at the table, which matters in wash-down areas and where a cord would be a hazard.

how_to_choose.title: Look for a maintenance prop
how_to_choose.text: Hydraulics hold a load at any height, which is the reason to choose them. If anyone will ever reach under the platform, the table needs a mechanical safety prop or maintenance bar — hydraulic pressure is not a substitute for a physical stop.

how_to_choose.title: Match the fluid to the environment
how_to_choose.text: Standard hydraulic oil is wrong for food production and for freezers. Food-grade fluid and low-temperature fluid are both normally available as options, but they have to be specified at order rather than swapped later.

how_to_choose.title: Ask what is serviceable in place
how_to_choose.text: Hoses, seals and the power unit are the parts that eventually need attention. A table whose power unit can be reached without lifting the platform is one a technician can fix on the floor instead of removing.

categories.description:
Electric lift tables use an electric motor, usually driving a hydraulic pump, to raise the platform at the press of a button or foot switch. They suit production work where a table is raised and lowered many times a shift and manual pumping would slow the operator down.

Motors range from single-phase units that plug into a standard outlet to three-phase motors for heavy or high-cycle tables. Compare voltage and phase against the power available at the workstation, the controls (hand pendant, foot switch or fixed push buttons), lift and lower speed, the rated duty cycle, and whether the electrical enclosure is suited to the environment.

how_to_choose.title: Confirm the supply before anything else
how_to_choose.text: Electric tables ship for a specific voltage and phase — commonly 115V single-phase or 230/460V three-phase. Getting this wrong means a transformer or a return, and it is the single most common ordering mistake in this category.

how_to_choose.title: Choose the control that fits the job
how_to_choose.text: A hand pendant suits an operator standing beside the table. A foot switch keeps both hands on the load. Fixed push buttons suit a fixed station. Constant-pressure controls — where the table stops the moment the button is released — matter wherever someone could be caught by the platform.

how_to_choose.title: Check the motor rating against the cycle rate
how_to_choose.text: Continuous-duty and intermittent-duty motors are priced differently for a reason. A table specified for intermittent duty and run continuously will overheat, and thermal cutouts stopping a line mid-shift is an expensive way to discover this.

how_to_choose.title: Corded or battery
how_to_choose.text: If the table stays put, mains power is simpler and cheaper. If it has to move, a battery unit removes the trailing cord, which is both a trip hazard and the part that fails first on a table that is dragged around.

categories.description:
Pneumatic lift tables are powered by compressed air, either through an air bag that inflates to lift the platform or an air motor that drives a hydraulic pump. Because they need no electricity at the table, they are chosen for spray booths and other areas where electrical equipment is not allowed, and for plants that already run compressed air to every workstation.

Air bag tables are simple and have few moving parts, while air-over-hydraulic designs give firmer, more precise positioning. Compare the required air pressure and flow against the shop supply, the controls, how the table holds its height under load, and the capacity and travel of the design.

Manual lift tables are raised by hand or foot, usually with a hydraulic foot pump, and need no power supply of any kind. That makes them inexpensive, self-contained and easy to move, and they are the standard choice for mobile lift carts and for workstations where a table is adjusted occasionally rather than cycled constantly.

The trade-off is effort and speed: every lift takes a number of pump strokes, which becomes tiring when a table is raised many times a day. Compare the number of strokes to full height, capacity, lowered and raised height, and how lowering is controlled. For frequent cycling, compare against electric, air or battery models.

categories.path: Lift Tables > Battery Powered Lift Tables
categories.description:
Battery powered lift tables carry their own rechargeable battery and pump, so they give push-button lifting with no power cord or air hose. They suit mobile tables that move around a facility, work far from electrical outlets, and outdoor use, while avoiding the repeated pumping of a manual table.

The battery powers a motor, usually driving a hydraulic pump, and is recharged from a standard outlet between shifts. Compare the number of lift cycles per charge, how long a full recharge takes, whether the charger is built in, how battery level is shown, and the capacity and travel of the table itself.
